title: The jackal's judgment
hookLine: two otters quarrel over a fish; the jackal judge takes the middle (Jataka 400)

lines: A FISH TOO BIG FOR ONE.
cards: On a riverbank, two otters are hunting together, one working the deep water, one along the shore. The deep-water otter bites into a huge fish, so strong it starts dragging him under.
He calls out, and his partner rushes in. Together they wrestle it onto the bank, and lie there panting, very pleased. Then one of them says: so, how do we split it?
That's where the Dabbhapuppha Jataka turns.

teach.b: First, the teamwork. Neither otter could have landed that fish alone; it took one in the deep and one on the shore. Second, the quarrel.
Now each is sure he deserves the better share. One caught it; the other saved him. Neither will give an inch, and the argument goes round and round.
A jackal comes down to drink, and the otters, tired of arguing, ask him to settle it. He's happy to oblige.
He gives the tail to the otter who worked the shore, and the head to the otter who went into the deep. The whole middle, the meat of the fish, he takes for himself as his fee for judging.
Off he trots, leaving the otters staring at a head and a tail. Fourth, the point.
Back home, the jackal's wife asks how a jackal who can't fish came by a fish like that, and his answer in the verse is blunt: quarrels make people thin, and the otters' quarrel fed him.

The tale's frame tells of a greedy monk who settled a dispute between two others over some robes, and kept the best one for himself. The jackal didn't have to fight or steal. The quarrel did the work for him.
If the otters had split the fish themselves, even unevenly, each would have eaten well. A fair settlement made by the people involved keeps the fish whole.

how: The monastic code, the Vinaya, sets out ways for monks and nuns to settle disputes within the community themselves, and this tale's frame is about a dispute settled badly.

o: a fee paid to settle a dispute
an argument neither side will drop
a fair deal split down the middle

games.q: the jackal's judgment: tap the pairs.
p: bit the fish and was dragged under
took the middle as his fee
asked where the fish came from

s: the jackal split the fish evenly
he gave one otter the tail, the other the head, and kept the middle.
the otters asked the jackal to judge
tired of arguing, they handed the decision to a stranger.
the jackal had to fight the otters for the fish
the quarrel did the work for him. he only had to be asked.

games.q: you're one of the otters. you and your partner can't agree how to split the fish, and a jackal offers to judge. what do you do?
o: split it between you, even if it's not perfect.
grab the whole fish and run.
games.why: in the tale the otters let the jackal judge, and he gave them the head and the tail and walked off with the middle.

practice: Take a small quarrel that's still open, over chores, money, or who said what, and sit with both sides as a fair judge would, not the jackal.
What's really yours, what's really theirs, and what's the middle being lost while the argument goes on? Breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Quarrel. What fed the jackal, called in to judge between two otters fighting over their catch, who walked off with the middle himself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the judge ate the fish. Quarrels make people thin, the jackal says. Until tomorrow.
